p.x:
I live on a busy street in Bangkok. Every morning, I walk to the bus stop near my house. There is always a lot of noise from cars and motorbikes.
On the corner, a woman sells noodles. Next to her, a man grills chicken. The smell is wonderful! I often buy breakfast there.
There is a small park with a bench and lots of pigeons. Old people sit there and feed the birds. A police officer stands at the crossing and helps children cross the road. I love my street because it is never boring.

In many Asian cities, the street is not just a place to walk; it is a place to live. In Bangkok, street food is everywhere. Vendors set up their stalls on the sidewalk early in the morning and sell everything from rice and curry to pork skewers and fresh fruit. In the evening, the night market opens, and the streetlights and neon signs make the area bright and colourful.
Getting around can be an adventure. Tourists love taking a tuk-tuk, although they often have to haggle over the price, since there is no price tag. Cyclists and pedestrians must watch out for potholes and puddles, especially in the rainy season when the drains overflow.
People find creative ways to cope with the heat. Shopkeepers put up umbrellas to create shade, and many people sit in small alleys where it is cooler. A busker might play guitar outside a station, while a security guard watches the entrance to a shopping centre.
In some neighbourhoods, old walls are covered with street art, and every shop has its own handwritten signboard. For many visitors, this busy, noisy street life is a big part of the city's charm.

Street vendors have long been part of urban life in Southeast Asia, but their future is increasingly uncertain. For millions of people, selling food or goods on the street is their main livelihood, and the informal economy provides cheap meals and jobs that the formal economy cannot. Yet city authorities often see hawkers as obstacles to modernisation, blaming them for blocking footpaths, creating litter and causing traffic problems.
In recent years, several cities have launched a crackdown on street selling. Vendors have been moved from busy roads, and some famous food streets have lost much of their character. Supporters argue that clearing the pavements makes cities safer and cleaner, allowing pedestrians to walk without stepping off the kerb into traffic and breathing in exhaust fumes. Critics reply that such policies punish the poor and destroy a valuable part of local culture.
The debate reflects a wider question about public space: who is it for? Urban regeneration projects frequently create pedestrianised streets and attractive plazas, but they may also include rules that discourage people from sitting, selling or simply loitering. Some cities have found a middle path. Singapore, for example, moved its hawkers into regulated food centres, preserving the tradition while improving hygiene.
Walk through an old neighbourhood in the evening, past a small shrine where incense burns, and it is easy to see why many residents value street life. The challenge is to keep cities orderly without losing their soul.
